title: Our Downloads Looked Great in the Deck. Our DAU/MAU Ratio Told the Real Story

Our DAU/MAU Ratio Told the Real Story GMTA Software Solutions Pvt Ltd 4 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Maya Chen had the download numbers every seed-stage founder wants in a pitch deck. Ledgerly, her personal budgeting app, was adding users steadily, acquisition cost was reasonable, and the App Store chart position looked good enough to screenshot. Revenue had been flat for two straight quarters, and Maya had spent most of that time assuming the fix was more top-of-funnel marketing spend. It wasn’t. It took a slow afternoon with her analytics dashboard to find the actual problem, and by then she’d already spent real money chasing the wrong number. The download chart looked healthy. The DAU/MAU ratio — the percentage of monthly active users who also opened the app on a given day — was sitting at 8%. Industry benchmarks put habitual daily-use products well above 20%. Ledgerly wasn’t a habit. It was something people downloaded, used once or twice to check a balance, and quietly forgot about until the next time a bill surprised them. The research that reframed the problem Maya’s first instinct was a notifications problem — get people to open the app more with better reminders. Her product lead pushed back with a wider point: the mobile market had matured past new-user acquisition as the primary growth lever, and the real competitive battleground had shifted to depth of use — how much of an already-acquired user’s time and habitual behavior an app could actually capture. Ledgerly had been optimizing entirely for the acquisition side of that equation and had no real answer for the other half. What the data actually showed: 8% DAU/MAU ratio — well below the roughly 20% threshold associated with habitual daily use 1.3 sessions/week average, and almost all of them on a single day rather than spread across the week 94% of active users had only ever touched the core expense-logging feature — the budgeting and savings-goal features, the ones actually built to create a reason to return, were nearly unused $0 additional engagement return on the marketing spend increase from the prior quarter, despite a real bump in downloads Founder takeaway: A rising download chart next to a flat revenue chart isn’t a marketing problem. It’s usually a sign the product was never actually built to be returned to — and no amount of acquisition spend fixes that. The rebuild Ledgerly’s team spent five weeks rebuilding around habit formation instead of activation. Onboarding changed from a single generic walkthrough to a first-week sequence that actively introduced the budgeting and goal-tracking features most users never found on their own. Notifications shifted from generic “check your balance” pings to context-aware nudges tied to actual spending patterns — the kind of prompt that gives someone a specific reason to open the app on a Tuesday, not just a reminder that the app exists. What actually changed 8% → 14% DAU/MAU ratio by month two 1.3 → 2.8 sessions per week, now spread across three or more distinct days instead of clustered on one 61% of active users had engaged with a second-layer feature (budgeting or goals) by month three, up from 6% +18% revenue growth in month three — the first quarter-over-quarter increase in over six months, without any change to acquisition spend Maya didn’t cut her marketing budget. She just stopped expecting it to solve a problem it was never going to solve. The download number had been telling her the acquisition engine worked. It had never been able to tell her whether anyone was actually building a habit around the product — and once she started measuring that separately, the fix was a product change, not a bigger ad budget. If your download chart and your revenue chart have stopped moving together, that gap is usually diagnosable with three numbers: DAU/MAU ratio, session frequency, and feature adoption depth. Most teams can measure acquisition cleanly but have no real system for catching a depth-of-use problem before it shows up as flat revenue a quarter later — which is exactly the gap GMTA’s own guide to predictive analytics in software development is built to close, using behavioral data you already have to forecast the drop-off instead of discovering it after the fact.
